overview: The MLX90640 is a genuine thermal imaging chip, not a single-point IR thermometer: it's a 32x24 grid of independent thermopile pixels, each one reading the actual temperature of whatever it's pointed at, all read out over a plain I2C bus. That low pixel count (768 total, versus millions on a visible-light sensor) is the honest trade for cost — a real FLIR-grade thermal sensor with useful resolution costs many times more — but it's still enough to pick out a person-shaped heat blob in total darkness, or spot a single overheating component on a board. Every chip ships with factory calibration constants in onboard EEPROM that must be read once and applied in software to convert raw pixel counts into actual degrees Celsius; skipping that step gives numbers that look plausible but are wrong.
simpleSummary: A low-resolution camera that sees heat instead of light, turning a room into a grid of temperature readings.

specifications.refreshRate: 0.5-64 Hz configurable (practical ceiling ~8-16Hz over standard I2C)
specifications.interface: I2C, address 0x33, up to 1MHz Fast Mode+
specifications.outputData: Raw 16-bit pixel array + factory EEPROM calibration constants, converted to °C in software

pinMap.name: VCC
pinMap.function: Power input for the sensor die and readout electronics.
pinMap.currentLimit: ~23 mA typical, higher during active frame capture
pinMap.gotcha: This sensor is 3.3V only on most bare breakouts — it is not 5V tolerant. Check your specific board for an onboard regulator before wiring it to a 5V rail.

pinMap.name: SDA
pinMap.function: I2C data line, used to read out the pixel frame and factory calibration constants.
pinMap.gotcha: Standard 100kHz I2C limits the usable refresh rate to just a few Hz. Getting anywhere near the sensor's higher refresh settings requires 1MHz Fast Mode+ I2C, which not every microcontroller or long wire run can drive reliably.

useCases.title: Person/animal presence detection in darkness
useCases.scenario: Spot a warm, person-shaped blob in a completely dark room without any visible-light illumination, preserving privacy since there's no recognizable image.

useCases.title: Predictive maintenance monitoring
useCases.scenario: Watch a motor, bearing, or electrical panel for abnormal hot spots that indicate developing failure before it happens.

useCases.title: Non-contact multi-point temperature check
useCases.scenario: Gauge temperature across several points on a moving part in one frame, instead of aiming a single-point IR thermometer repeatedly.

useCases.title: Warehouse patrol robot fire/hotspot warning
useCases.scenario: Continuously scan for abnormal heat sources as an early-warning layer on a patrolling robot.

useCases.title: Low-cost heat-blob gesture tracking
useCases.scenario: Track a hand's coarse position by its heat signature as a cheap alternative to a depth camera for close-range interaction.

commonlyPairedWith: SSD1306 OLED (for visualizing the thermal grid)
oftenConfusedWith: PIR Motion Sensor (a PIR only outputs a binary 'something's heat signature changed' trigger; this sensor outputs a real 32x24 grid of actual temperature values, showing shape and intensity, not just a yes/no)
Intel RealSense D435i / Stereo Camera Module (measure distance/depth, not temperature)
oftenUpgradedTo: FLIR Lepton (160x120 resolution, SPI/VoSPI video-style interface, true radiometric imaging quality instead of a coarse grid)

beginnerMistakes: Powering it at 5V directly instead of 3.3V, damaging the sensor.
Expecting a sharp 'picture' — 768 pixels produces a coarse heat blob, not a photo-quality thermal image.
Not letting the sensor thermally stabilize for a few seconds after power-on before trusting absolute readings.
Placing it behind glass or plastic — most common materials are opaque to the long-wave infrared this sensor reads, producing a flat or misleading reading.
Pushing the refresh rate higher than the I2C bus speed in use can sustain, causing frame reads to return stale or torn pixel data.
